details:
**Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair**
Neruda's breakthrough 1924 collection, published when he was 19. It contains twenty numbered love poems followed by one final despairing poem, and it is by far the most common title clue and giveaway for him.

**"In you everything sank!"**
The refrain of "The Song of Despair," the closing poem of Twenty Love Poems. The speaker addresses a lost lover, calling her a "pit of debris" into which all his hopes fell.

**"Tonight I can write the saddest lines"**
The opening of Poem 20, the last of the twenty love poems, which comes just before "The Song of Despair." As examples of sad lines, the speaker offers "The night is starry" and "the night wind revolves in the sky and sings." The poem includes "She loved me, sometimes I loved her too" and "Love is so short, forgetting is so long," and it ends hoping this will be "the last pain that she makes me suffer."

**"It is the hour of departure"**
The other refrain of "The Song of Despair," which opens "The memory of you emerges from the night around me." The speaker, "deserted like the wharves at dawn," recalls the lover as a "cemetery of kisses" and says "There were thirst and hunger, and you were the fruit. / There were grief and the ruins, and you were the miracle."

**"Body of a Woman"**
Poem 1 of Twenty Love Poems, which begins "Body of a woman, white hills, white thighs, / you look like a world, lying in surrender." The speaker says he was "alone like a tunnel" and "forged you like a weapon" to survive, and his "rough peasant's body" digs into hers.

**Elemental Odes**
Neruda's 1950s collections of odes in short, plain lines that celebrate everyday things. Subjects include the onion, which can "make us cry without hurting us"; tomatoes, which "invade the kitchen" in summer; conger chowder; artichokes; socks; and a large tuna in the market.

**"Ode to My Socks"**
An elemental ode about a pair of woolen socks knitted for him by Maru Mori. He compares his feet in them to "two fish," "two long sharks," "two immense blackbirds," and "two cannons," and ends by saying that "beauty is twice beauty / and what is good is doubly good" when it comes to two wool socks in winter.

**"White Bee"**
A poem from Twenty Love Poems that begins "White bee, you buzz in my soul, drunk with honey" and repeats the refrain "Ah you who are silent!" The speaker calls himself "the one without hope, the word without echoes" and tells the beloved, "In my barren land you are the final rose."

**Canto General and "The Heights of Macchu Picchu"**
Neruda's 1950 epic history of the Americas, which includes sections such as "The Conquistadors," "The Liberators," and "America, I Do Not Invoke Your Name in Vain." He wrote much of it in hiding after the Chilean government persecuted him as a Communist, before fleeing over the Andes in 1949. Its most famous section, "The Heights of Macchu Picchu," begins by moving "from air to air, like an empty net" and ends with "Arise to birth with me, my brother," asking the dead workers to "speak through my words and my blood."

**"Ode to the Artichoke"**
An elemental ode that pictures the "tender-hearted" artichoke as a soldier "dressed as a warrior" in armor among the frail vegetables of the garden. At the end, María buys it at the market along with shoes, a white cabbage, and a bottle of vinegar, and cooks and eats it leaf by leaf.

**"Every Day You Play"**
Poem 14 of Twenty Love Poems, which opens "Every day you play with the light of the universe." The speaker offers to bring "rustic baskets of kisses" and closes with "I want to do with you what spring does with the cherry trees."

**"United Fruit Company"**
A political poem from Canto General attacking the American fruit company. It begins with a trumpet sounding and Jehovah parceling out the world to "Coca-Cola Inc., Anaconda, Ford Motors," while United Fruit takes the "central coast" of the Americas, the "Banana Republics." It mocks the dictators it props up as flies, accusing the company of having "abolished free will."

**"A Dog Has Died"**
A late poem that begins with the speaker burying his dead dog in the garden "next to a rusted old machine," adding that "some day I'll join him right there." Though he has "never believed in any promised heaven in the sky," he believes "in a heaven I'll never enter."

**"Walking Around"**
A poem from Neruda's surrealist collection Residence on Earth, opening "It so happens I am sick of being a man." The speaker fantasizes that it would be marvelous "to terrify a law clerk with a cut lily, / or kill a nun with a blow on the ear."

**"Ah Vastness of Pines"**
Poem 3 of Twenty Love Poems, which opens "Ah vastness of pines, murmur of waves breaking." The speaker tells the beloved, "In you the rivers sing and my soul flees in them as you desire."
